body: These examples separate normalized from unnormalized leakage, compute a finite binary privacy–utility objective and its perfect-privacy boundary, and evaluate a degraded binary erasure wiretap channel. Each calculation uses finite alphabets and natural-log nats.

This page begins with a general sequence of measurable channel kernels whose input and output spaces may vary by blocklength, then specializes to a fixed finite DMC with product transition law. Codes use a uniform message for average error and also record maximal error; rates are in nats per use. No feedback or input-cost constraint is imposed. The capacity proof gives finite-alphabet random-coding achievability, an entropy/Fano converse, and the strong converse using a capacity-achieving output law and a likelihood threshold.

The diagram denotes the conditional kernel carrying an input word to an output law. For a DMC, its exact probabilities are $W^n(y^n\mid x^n)=\prod_iW(y_i\mid x_i)$ as defined and proved above; the arrow is not a deterministic map.

```tikzcd
\mathcal X^n \arrow[r, "W^n"] & \mathcal Y^n
```

These calculations apply the finite-DMC capacity formula to binary symmetric and binary erasure channels. They use natural logarithms and include the deterministic, fully erased, and fully noisy endpoints.

Average and maximal error can differ for a finite code. For one use of the BEC with erasure probability $\epsilon$, send messages $1,2$ as $0,1$ and decode $0,1,\star$ as $1,2,1$, respectively, where $\star$ denotes erasure. The two message error probabilities are $0$ and $\epsilon$, so the uniform-message average error is $\epsilon/2$ while the maximal error is $\epsilon$ ([[def-fixed-length-channel-code-errors]], [[ex-binary-erasure-channel-capacity]]). In general, average error is at most maximal error; the expurgation lemma retains at least half the messages with maximal error at most twice the original average error ([[lem-discrete-memoryless-channel-average-to-maximal-expurgation]]). These finite-code criteria nevertheless give the same asymptotic capacity: the A-page theorem proves $C_{\rm av}(W)=C_{\max}(W)=C(W)$ for every finite DMC without a cost constraint ([[thm-discrete-memoryless-channel-capacity-formula]]).

This page develops finite-DMC capacity under a nonnegative letter cost, including the boundary budget equal to the minimum letter cost. It then treats finite-dimensional additive Gaussian channels under expected average squared power, diagonalizes correlated Gaussian noise by an orthogonal change of coordinates, and proves the water-filling formula for both ordinary and causal-feedback codes. All logarithms and rates are in natural nats; the Gaussian law and its orthogonal invariance are used under AC. The random-coding arguments use threshold decoding and explicitly prune codewords that violate the per-codeword cost. A separate countable-input, finite-output, zero-cost DMC definition supports the companion example about nonattainment; it does not alter the finite-alphabet capacity theorem.

The diagram records the causal interface at a single use. The encoder receives the finite message and the history of outputs from earlier uses; the channel kernel then produces the current output. In the Gaussian case the kernel is translation by fresh independent noise, while in a finite DMC it is the row $W(\cdot\mid X_t)$. The feedback arrow represents that past history, not the current output, and the proofs establish the capacity bounds without relying on the diagram.

```tikzcd
M \arrow[r, "f_t(M,Y^{t-1})"] & X_t \arrow[r, "\text{channel kernel}"] & Y_t \\
\mathcal Y^{t-1} \arrow[ur, "\text{past-output history}"'] &&
```

These examples compute a binary identity channel's capacity under a unit letter cost, solve both regimes of the two-branch AWGN water-filling allocation, diagonalize an explicit correlated Gaussian noise covariance, and exhibit a countable-input DMC whose finite information-capacity supremum is not attained. The countable-input example uses the separately defined countable-input model and proves directly that its finite information-capacity supremum has no maximizing input law. All examples use nats and verify relevant endpoints. The Gaussian and binary identity examples also identify when feedback leaves capacity unchanged.

These examples evaluate the one-shot dependence-testing expression and meta-converse on a binary symmetric channel, then give a finite noiseless-channel counterexample separating small average error from maximal error. The calculations retain the null/alternative convention for $\beta_\epsilon$ and distinguish average-error bounds from per-message guarantees.

All alphabets and probability laws on this page are finite, and information is measured in natural-log nats as in [[def-it-information-units-and-logarithm-base]]. A wiretap channel has one input and two outputs whose conditional dependence is retained in the joint kernel:

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}
& Y \\
X \arrow[ur, "W_Y"] \arrow[dr, "W_Z"'] & \\
& Z
\end{tikzcd}
```

The two arrows label the Bob and Eve marginals of the joint law $W(y,z\mid x)$. They do not assert that $Y$ and $Z$ are conditionally independent given $X$. The block law is the coordinate product of this joint kernel. A code uses a uniform message, private encoder randomness and no feedback or preshared secret key; its public description is available to Eve.

Information leakage and equivocation are defined in [[def-it-information-leakage-and-equivocation]]. Weak secrecy requires $I(M;Z^n)/n\to0$, while strong secrecy requires $I(M;Z^n)\to0$, as in [[def-it-weak-and-strong-secrecy]]. Strong secrecy implies weak secrecy, but the converse fails; the companion page gives a noiseless example. Capacity here is defined operationally for both average and maximal error, and for both secrecy criteria. The local finite information-density lemma supports fixed-auxiliary threshold decoding, while the resolvability lemma makes Eve's induced output law approach a product target in expected KL and total variation. The capacity theorem proves the same auxiliary formula for all four capacities:

$$\max_{P_{U,X}:\,U-X-(Y,Z)}\bigl[I(U;Y)-I(U;Z)\bigr],\qquad |\mathcal U|\le|\mathcal X|.$$

For a degraded channel in the sense of [[def-it-degraded-wiretap-channel]], Eve's output is generated from Bob's by a finite stochastic kernel, the auxiliary reduces to $U=X$, and the formula becomes $\max_{P_X}[I(X;Y)-I(X;Z)]$.

For finite source privacy in [[def-it-finite-source-privacy-utility-region]], a release kernel gives the factorization $P_{SXZ}=P_{SX}K_{Z\mid X}$:

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}
S \arrow[r] & X \arrow[r, "K"] & Z
\end{tikzcd}
```

The privacy–utility coordinates are $(I(S;Z),I(X;Z))$: the first measures leakage about sensitive data and the second measures retained information about useful data. Perfect privacy is exactly equality of the conditional output laws across positive-support sensitive values, by [[thm-it-perfect-privacy-kernel-criterion]]. This criterion is a kernel condition and does not impose a distortion or rate constraint.

Universal hashing is treated separately by [[thm-it-universal-hashing-leftover-bound]] as a total-variation guarantee with the public seed included alongside Eve's side information. For conditional guessing probability $g(X\mid Z)$ and an $M$-valued two-universal hash, the bound is $\operatorname{TV}\le\tfrac12\sqrt{M g(X\mid Z)}$; in particular, $M g(X\mid Z)\le4\varepsilon^2$ guarantees distance at most $\varepsilon$. This bound does not by itself state an unnormalized mutual-information guarantee.

These examples compute a strict entropy-capacity budget for a finite IID source and a BSC, then show the limit of that asymptotic result. A full-support noisy channel has positive error at every finite blocklength for any nontrivial source, even when the asymptotic separation inequality is strict. The examples distinguish asymptotic reliability from finite-block zero-error performance.
